items.prompt: Which of these is a feature of a backpack?
choices: It has padded shoulder straps
Your shoulders hurt less on the walk
You can carry books without strain
The walk home feels shorter today
items.explanation: Padded straps are a fact about the product. The other lines describe what the wearer experiences.

items.prompt: Which of these is a value statement about a drill?
choices: The shelf stays up with all your books
It has an eighteen-volt battery pack
The chuck opens without any key
It ships with a carrying case
items.explanation: Only the shelf line describes what changes for the listener. The rest are product facts.

items.prompt: A feature is best described as
choices: A fact about what the product has or does
A reason the listener wants to buy it
A promise about how the listener will feel
A price the seller chooses to charge
items.explanation: A feature is a property of the product, true whoever is listening.

items.prompt: Value is best described as
choices: What a feature changes for one listener
A longer list of the product's specifications
The highest price a seller could ever charge
A fact that is true for every single listener
items.explanation: Value is relative to the listener and their goal.

items.prompt: 'This umbrella has fibreglass ribs' is
choices: A feature, because it states a material
Value, because it names a real part
Value, because the ribs are strong
A promise, because ribs are important
items.explanation: It names what the umbrella is made of and says nothing about the listener's day.

items.prompt: 'You stay dry in a strong gust' is
choices: Value, since it states the listener's outcome
A feature, since it is a plainly true claim
A feature, since it mentions the weather
A spec, since wind speed can be measured
items.explanation: It describes what happens to the listener, in everyday words.

items.prompt: Does a feature change depending on who is listening?
choices: No, it is the same for every listener
Yes, it adapts itself to each new listener
Only when the listener happens to be an expert
Only when the product's price is also mentioned
items.explanation: Features are facts about the product. Value is what depends on the listener.

items.prompt: Which pair is correctly labelled feature then value?
choices: 10-cup capacity; fewer refills during dinner
Fewer refills during dinner; 10-cup capacity
Dishwasher-safe lid; a lid with a clean seal
Free shipping; an order that arrives soon
items.explanation: The first item states a fact, and the second states what it changes for the person using it.

items.prompt: A seller says: 'The vacuum has a 1,200-watt motor.' A listener asks why that matters. Which reply is a value statement?
choices: The motor is rated higher than most competing vacuum motors
Floors get clean in one pass, so you finish the room faster
The motor draws more power than the model it replaces
The motor is sealed in a housing to cut noise and dust
items.explanation: Only the first reply turns the motor into an outcome for the listener (time saved). The others are further product facts.
items.reference:
Fact versus change
🔧 Feature: a fact about the product, same for every listener
🕳️ Value: what that fact changes for this listener
Why: a feature describes the product, while value describes the listener's own outcome.
items.learnMore:
A feature is a fact; value is the change it makes

The same drill is an 18-volt tool to one person and a shelf that stays up to another. Value is always relative to what the listener is trying to do.

Common mistake

Assuming that a more impressive spec is the same thing as a stronger reason to care.
items.reflection: Think of the last thing you bought. Which feature did you never understand, and what change in your life made you buy it anyway?

items.prompt: Two people hear the same drill pitch: one is hanging a shelf, one is building a deck. What stays the same and what changes?
choices: The value stays the same; the features each person hears differ
The features stay the same; the value each hears differs
Both the features and the value differ with each person's need
Both the features and the value stay identical for both people
items.explanation: Features belong to the product. Value depends on what each listener needs done.

items.prompt: Which sentence is hardest to classify as purely a feature, and why?
choices: 'Weighs 2 kilograms' states a pure number and nothing more
'Battery lasts 8 hours' states a spec but hints at saved time
'Made of steel' names a material and no outcome at all
'Has a red handle' names a colour and no outcome at all
items.explanation: A spec can lean toward value when it implies an outcome, but without saying who benefits it is still a product fact. The others have no outcome at all.

items.prompt: The translation gap is
choices: The time a product takes to be delivered
The work between a feature and a reason to care
A mistake in translating one language to another
The difference between two competing prices
items.explanation: It is the mental work a listener must do to connect a fact to why it matters.

items.prompt: Here, 'translation' means
choices: Converting each word from one language into another
Turning a technical fact into something usable
Rewriting a long sentence into a much shorter form
Copying a specification from the manual word for word
items.explanation: The unit uses translation for turning facts into a reason to care, not for languages.

items.prompt: With feature framing, who does the translation?
choices: The speaker
The listener
A hired translator
Nobody at all
items.explanation: Feature framing hands over a fact and leaves the listener to work out why it matters.

items.prompt: With value framing, who does the translation?
choices: The listener
The speaker
The product's manual
The seller's competitor
items.explanation: The speaker builds the bridge from fact to reason, so the listener does not have to.

items.prompt: What does a wide translation gap usually cause?
choices: Most listeners ask many follow-up questions
Most listeners give up before crossing it
Most listeners buy the product at once
Most listeners remember every spec
items.explanation: Crossing a wide gap takes effort, and most people do not spend it.

items.prompt: Why can't a listener 'just figure it out'?
choices: They are usually too lazy to think
They often lack the background to see why it matters
They are usually too busy to listen
They are not allowed to ask questions
items.explanation: The listener's missing background is the issue, not their ability.

items.prompt: Which sentence has the narrowest translation gap?
choices: '18-volt brushless motor'
'Your shelf stays up tonight'
'Keyless chuck, 13 millimetre'
'Variable torque clutch'
items.explanation: It is already in terms the listener uses. The others need background to interpret.

items.prompt: What is a pitch?
choices: A long manual covering every feature
A short explanation meant to make someone care
A price list sorted by product type
A technical report on product testing
items.explanation: A pitch is brief and aims at getting the listener to care enough to continue.

items.prompt: A speaker lists six impressive specs and the listener says 'OK' and walks away. Which is the most likely explanation?
choices: The listener thought that the specs were too few in number
The listener disliked the speaker's tone of voice and manner
The listener could not turn any spec into a reason
The listener wanted a lower price before deciding anything
items.explanation: Specs leave the translation work to the listener. Without background, the polite 'OK' means the gap was too wide.
items.reference:
Who builds the bridge?
🧱 Feature framing: the listener builds the bridge
🌉 Value framing: the speaker builds the bridge
🚪 Gap too wide: the listener stops listening
Why: a wider gap means fewer listeners finish the work of reaching the reason to care.
items.learnMore:
The translation gap is work, and most people skip work

A listener who lacks the background cannot tell which features matter. Value framing moves the translation work from the listener to the speaker, who is better placed to do it.

Common mistake

Believing that a smart listener will fill the gap alone. Intelligence is not the issue; missing background is.
items.reflection: Recall a time you stopped listening to an explanation. Which step were you expected to fill in yourself?

items.prompt: Why can adding more features to a pitch widen the translation gap?
choices: Each extra feature raises the price the listener expects
Each extra feature makes the speaker sound less confident
Each extra feature is another fact the listener must translate
Each extra feature shortens the time the listener has
items.explanation: More facts means more translation work, not less. The gap grows with every unexplained spec.

choices: The listener, who knows their own situation but not the product
A third party, who knows neither side well enough to bridge it
The speaker, who knows both the product and the listener's goal
Nobody, since translation cannot be done before a purchase
items.explanation: The speaker has the product knowledge, and by asking about the listener's goal can add the other half.

items.prompt: What question moves you up the ladder?
choices: 'How much does it cost to build?'
'Who else sells something like this?'
'So what does that mean for the listener?'
'What is the product's model number?'
items.explanation: That question shifts attention from the product to the listener's outcome.

items.prompt: At the bottom of the ladder you find
choices: A promise about the listener's future
A comparison with a competing product
A spec, a plain fact about the product
A figure for the listener's savings
items.explanation: Step 1 is the product fact. Value sits at the top.

items.prompt: At the top of the ladder you find
choices: A longer and more detailed list of technical terms
The single most precise measurement of the product
Something the listener already cares about
The full name of the company that made the product
items.explanation: The top is expressed in money, time, comfort, risk or effort.

items.prompt: Each step on the ladder is
choices: Invented to make the pitch sound better
Removed once the next step is reached
True, with the focus moving to the listener
Optional unless the product is expensive
items.explanation: Nothing is made up. Only the fact that is said aloud changes.

items.prompt: In 'it has X, that causes Y, so you get Z', Z is
choices: The feature
The bridge
The value
The price
items.explanation: X is the feature, Y the bridge, and Z the value.

items.prompt: In the same shape, X is
choices: The value
The bridge
The feature
The listener
items.explanation: X is where you start: a fact about the product.

items.prompt: Which of these is a term the listener already understands?
choices: Chlorine adsorption
Activated carbon
Money
Filter micron rating
items.explanation: Money, time, comfort, risk and effort need no product background.

items.prompt: 'Tastes close to bottled water' sits
choices: Lower than 'activated carbon filter'
At the very top of the ladder
Higher than 'removes chlorine'
Outside the ladder altogether
items.explanation: It compares the result to something the listener knows, so it is closer to value.

items.prompt: A pitch says 'rated for 40 gallons per filter.' Which next rung is the best 'so what' step?
choices: The rating comes from standard laboratory testing
Forty gallons is a larger unit than ten cups
Each filter has the same shape as the last one
You replace the filter only a few times a year
items.explanation: The best step turns the spec into an effect on the listener (fewer replacements). The others add more facts about the product.
items.reference:
The ladder, from spec to outcome
1️⃣ Spec: activated carbon filter
2️⃣ Effect: removes chlorine and sediment
3️⃣ Sense: no chlorine taste
4️⃣ Compare: close to bottled water
5️⃣ Value: stop buying bottles, save money
Why: keep asking 'so what?' until the answer is something the listener already cares about.
items.learnMore:
Repeat 'so what does that mean for them?'

Each rung stays true; only the focus moves from the product to the listener. The shape it has X, that causes Y, so you get Z gives a quick way to check whether you reached the top.

Common mistake

Stopping at a rung that sounds impressive but is still product vocabulary.
items.reflection: Pick something you use every day. Climb its ladder from a spec to a result in your own life. Where does it first feel personal?

items.prompt: A speaker's ladder ends at 'it removes 99% of particles.' Why has the climb not finished?

Particles are not something the listener is likely to care about
The speaker should have started with this sentence at the top
The listener still has to work out why that matters to them
items.explanation: A percentage about the product is still a product fact. The climb ends only when the statement is in the listener's own terms.

items.prompt: The curse of knowledge is a bias where
choices: You forget facts you learned long ago
You trust the first number you hear
You prefer the explanation you heard first
You forget how hard it is not to know something
items.explanation: Knowing something makes it hard to imagine the view of someone who does not.

items.prompt: Who is most affected by it?
choices: People who have just met the product
People who dislike the product
People who are shopping for gifts
People who know the product best
items.explanation: Deep familiarity is exactly what hides the listener's gap.

items.prompt: What does the bias cause in a pitch?
choices: Too many value statements arriving one after another
Too many questions being asked of the listener directly
Too much attention paid to the listener's likely budget
Skipped middle steps, so the pitch stops at the spec
items.explanation: Experts treat the middle steps as obvious and leave them out.

items.prompt: The bias is cured by
choices: Making sure you know much less about the product
Choosing longer and more technical words to be safe
Waiting until after the listener has asked questions
Climbing the ladder on purpose every time
items.explanation: The remedy is a deliberate habit, not forgetting.

items.prompt: A classmate cannot divide fractions yet. The expert classmate
choices: Remembers that every step needs writing out
Refuses to explain any steps at all
Writes extra steps no one asked for
Forgets that every step needs writing out
items.explanation: The fractions example shows the same bias: what is easy to you feels obvious to everyone.

items.prompt: Is the bias a sign of carelessness?
choices: Yes, it comes from deliberate laziness
Yes, it comes from not knowing enough
No, it only happens to new employees
No, the skipped steps genuinely feel obvious
items.explanation: The speaker is not lazy. The steps seem too obvious to say.

items.prompt: Which speaker is most likely to skip steps?
choices: A reviewer who tried it for the first time
A customer who bought it yesterday
A shopper reading the box in a store
A specialist who has used the product for years
items.explanation: Long familiarity makes the specs feel self-explanatory.

items.prompt: Which check best exposes the bias?
choices: Read the spec sheet out loud to yourself in private
Ask a close colleague to proofread the written spec
Count how many technical terms appear in the pitch
Explain it to someone with no background and watch
items.explanation: A listener without background shows where the gap actually is.

items.prompt: An engineer says 'it has 99.9% uptime' and expects applause. Which explanation fits the curse of knowledge?
choices: She lives with the metric and no longer sees the gap
She chose a number so high that it cannot be understood by anyone
She knows the number is false but states it in order to impress
She believes that listeners always prefer percentages to plain words
items.explanation: The bias is that familiarity hides the gap. She is not lying or showing off; the link to downtime feels obvious to her.
items.reference:
Why experts skip the middle
🧠 Expert: knows every spec by heart
🙈 Bias: cannot picture not knowing it
⏭️ Result: skips the middle ladder steps
Why: knowing a thing well makes it hard to see how much explanation others need.
items.learnMore:
Once you know it, you can't unknow it

The expert is not careless; the missing steps feel too obvious to say. The cure is a habit of climbing the ladder deliberately.

Common mistake

Trying to cure the bias by knowing less. It is cured by checking with the listener, not by forgetting.
items.reflection: Where have you explained something you know well and watched a listener get lost? Which step did you skip because it felt obvious?

items.prompt: Why does asking the speaker to 'just explain it more simply' often fail?
choices: They cannot tell which steps the listener is missing
They do not have enough time to explain anything
They have usually forgotten how the product works
They believe the listener would rather not hear it
items.explanation: The speaker's difficulty is spotting the gap, so simply trying harder does not help. The fix is feedback from a real listener.

items.explanation: Customer vocabulary tells you what the top of the ladder sounds like. The ladder still supplies the steps to get there.

items.prompt: 'Improves hydration compliance metrics' is
choices: A feature dressed in value language
A clear statement of everyday value
A statement of the product's price
A claim about the listener's budget
items.explanation: The listener still has to translate 'compliance metrics' into something personal.

items.prompt: Value framing must also be
choices: Accurate
Long
Technical
Cheaper
items.explanation: A persuasive claim that is false sets up disappointment.

items.prompt: 'Saves $1,028.50 in year one' holds only if
choices: The listener buys bottles at the assumed rate
The listener has already bought a pitcher once before
The listener lives somewhere with a very cold climate
The listener prefers the taste of filtered water
items.explanation: The figure depends on two bottles a day at $1.50. Another habit gives another number.

items.prompt: Which is audience-relevant?
choices: 'You spend less each month'
'Optimises hydration KPIs'
'Reduces particulate ppm'
'Increases throughput'
items.explanation: Money in everyday words needs no product background.

items.prompt: Which failure is listed at this level?
choices: Assuming the listener will climb the ladder alone
Writing a pitch that turns out to be much too short
Mentioning the product's price far too early on
Using a tone of voice that is much too friendly
items.explanation: Most listeners will not climb alone, which is the first failure listed.

items.prompt: A claim that sounds like a benefit but needs translation is
choices: Still a feature
Value, because of its tone
A promise, because it is vague
A spec, because it has numbers
items.explanation: Judge a claim by whether the listener can use it directly.

items.prompt: Which statement is more checkable?
choices: '$1,028.50 less this year'
'Saves you a lot of money'
'Great value for the price'
'Better than the usual choice'
items.explanation: A specific figure can be verified, so it is more trustworthy.

items.prompt: Climbing 'too far' means
choices: Claiming something that is no longer true
Using too many ladder rungs
Mentioning the product's name often
Speaking for longer than a minute
items.explanation: Value framing must stay accurate; overreaching claims lose trust.

items.prompt: A pitch claims 'you will save $1,028.50' to a listener who drinks two glasses of tap water a day. What is wrong with it?
choices: The figure is too small for it to be worth stating at all
The figure rests on a bottle habit this listener lacks
The figure should have been given as a percentage instead
The figure should have come before any mention of taste
items.explanation: Value framing must be true for the actual listener. The assumed habit, two bottles a day, is missing here.
items.reference:
Three ways the climb goes wrong
⏸️ Listener left to climb alone
📈 Climb past what is true
🎭 Feature wearing value language
Why: a value claim must be both audience-relevant and accurate to the listener's real situation.
items.learnMore:
Value language must be true and in the listener's terms

Saying 'saves you money' without a basis is a promise, not a value. And phrases like hydration compliance metrics only sound like value; the listener must still translate them.

Common mistake

Judging a statement by how benefit-like it sounds rather than whether the listener can use it directly.

items.prompt: Bottled water for a year at $1.50 x 2 x 365 costs
items.explanation: 1.50 times 2 is 3.00 per day, and 3.00 times 365 is 1,095.

items.prompt: Water filtered in a year at 0.5 gallons a day is
choices: 73 gallons
182.5 gallons
365 gallons
1,825 gallons

items.prompt: At 40 gallons per filter, a year uses about
choices: 0.22 filters
4.56 filters
9.13 filters
45.6 filters
items.explanation: 182.5 divided by 40 is 4.5625.

items.prompt: Filters cost $8 each, so a year of filters costs
Pitcher plus filters in year one costs
items.explanation: The one-time $30 plus the $36.50 of filters.

items.prompt: A one-time cost is
choices: Paid again each year, like a filter
Paid once, like buying the pitcher
Paid monthly, like a subscription
Paid only if the product breaks
items.explanation: One-time costs land in year one only.

items.prompt: A recurring cost is
choices: One that is paid at the very start of use only
One that comes back, like filters or bottles
One that is paid at the very end of use only
One that never belongs in a cost comparison
items.explanation: Recurring costs repeat for each period.

items.prompt: Year-one saving is bottles minus pitcher plus filters, or
From year two onward, what does the yearly comparison use?
items.explanation: The pitcher is already bought, so only the recurring costs remain: bottles against filters.
items.reference:
Year-one arithmetic
🥤 Bottles: $1.50 x 2 x 365 = $1,095.00
🚰 Filters: 4.5625 x $8 = $36.50
💲 Pitcher: $30 one-time
✅ Year one: $1,095.00 - $66.50 = $1,028.50
Why: a one-time cost lands in year one only, while recurring costs repeat every year.
items.learnMore:
One-time costs and recurring costs behave differently

The pitcher is paid once. Filters and bottles come back every year. Mixing them in one yearly figure overstates later years.

Common mistake

Charging the one-time cost to every year, or ignoring that a filter is rated for volume rather than time.
items.reflection: Pick a recurring subscription of yours. What would its first year, and its later years, look like if a one-time set-up cost applied?

items.prompt: Three-year cumulative cost of the pitcher is $139.50. How is it built?
choices: $30 for each of three years, plus $36.50 once only
$66.50 for each of the three years in a row
$30 once, then $36.50 for each of three years
$36.50 once only, then $30 for each of three years
items.explanation: 30 + 3 x 36.50 = 139.50. The pitcher is a one-time cost and the filters recur.
items.reference:
Year-one arithmetic
🥤 Bottles: $1.50 x 2 x 365 = $1,095.00
🚰 Filters: 4.5625 x $8 = $36.50
💲 Pitcher: $30 one-time
✅ Year one: $1,095.00 - $66.50 = $1,028.50
Why: a one-time cost lands in year one only, while recurring costs repeat every year.

items.prompt: Which change would most reduce the $1,028.50 figure?
choices: The filter price goes up by a single dollar per filter
The pitcher price goes up by a single dollar in total
The listener buys one bottle a day, not two
The filter rating falls by one gallon per filter
items.explanation: Bottle volume scales the biggest term (half of 1,095 is 547.50). The other changes move only small costs.

items.prompt: Pitch A tells the listener about
choices: The yearly saving and the taste of the water
The filter, capacity and plastic type
The bottled-water comparison for one whole year
The three-year cumulative gap between the costs
items.explanation: Pitch A states product facts. Pitch B states outcomes.

items.prompt: Pitch B leads with
choices: The filter material and its fine grade
Taste and a dollar saving
The grade of plastic used for the pitcher
The pitcher's capacity measured in cups
items.explanation: It states outcomes in terms the listener already uses.

items.prompt: Are the facts in Pitch B invented?
choices: Yes, they are made up in order to persuade
No, they come from the same facts
Yes, they replace the real specs of the product
Only the dollar figures are made up by the seller
items.explanation: Both pitches draw on the same fixed facts.

items.prompt: The year-three gap in the unit is
Pitch A leaves out
choices: Any mention of the filter
Any dollar figure
Any mention of capacity
Any mention of the material
items.explanation: It never computes the saving, so the listener must.

items.prompt: Does value framing mean never mentioning features?
choices: Yes, features must never be mentioned in a pitch
No, features follow once the listener is curious
Yes, features are always false in a value pitch
No, features should always be said before value
items.explanation: Value leads; features answer follow-up questions.

items.prompt: A listener asks how it works. A good reply gives
choices: More value language repeated
An accurate feature-level answer
A change of subject to price
A refusal to explain
items.explanation: A curious listener deserves an accurate answer.

items.prompt: Why is Pitch B more persuasive than A?
choices: It is more excited than Pitch A
It did the arithmetic the listener would not do
It is longer than Pitch A
It uses more technical words
items.explanation: Persuasion comes from doing the translation work, not from enthusiasm.

items.prompt: After three years the bottled-water total is $3,285.00. What does the pitcher total look like, and why?
choices: $109.50: $36.50 once plus $36.50 for each further year
$199.50: $66.50 for each of the three years in turn
$139.50: $30 once plus $36.50 for each of three years
$99.00: $33 for each of the three years in turn
items.explanation: 30 + 3 x 36.50 = 139.50. The pitcher is bought once and filters repeat annually.
items.reference:
Pitch A versus Pitch B
🅰️ A: carbon filter, 10 cups, BPA-free; listener translates
🅱️ B: tastes like bottled water; $1,028 less in year one
📊 Year three: $3,285.00 against $139.50
Why: the value pitch does the arithmetic the feature pitch leaves for the listener.
items.learnMore:
The arithmetic is what persuades

Pitch B is not more excited; it computed the figure the listener would not compute alone. The features can follow once the listener is curious.

Common mistake

Concluding that value framing means features are never mentioned. They simply follow the value.
items.reflection: Take a pitch you have heard recently. Which figure did the speaker leave for you to work out?

items.prompt: A listener asks 'but how does the filter work?' after hearing Pitch B. What is the best response?
choices: Repeat the saving figure until they finally accept it
Explain that features do not matter to most buyers
Give an accurate feature explanation; they are now curious
Offer a discount to end the question as quickly as possible
items.explanation: Value gets attention; accurate features then support the interested listener. Dodging the question damages trust.

items.prompt: The $1,028.50 saving assumes
choices: Four bottles a day at $1.50
One bottle a day at $3.00
Two bottles a day at $1.50
No bottles are bought at all
items.explanation: The bottle habit is an assumed input, not a universal fact.

items.prompt: A listener who never buys bottles
choices: Saves more than any other kind of listener
Saves exactly $1,028.50 in the first year
Cannot realise the bottled-water saving
Saves nothing at all on every other product
items.explanation: The saving comes from replacing bottles.

items.prompt: In the interactive demo, 0 bottles a day gives
choices: A saving of $66.50 in the first year
A saving of $1,028.50 in the first year
A loss of $66.50 in year one
A saving of $0.00 in the first year
items.explanation: The pitcher costs $66.50 in year one and replaces nothing.

items.prompt: The method for a different listener is
choices: Quote the same headline figure
Remove all the numbers
Find what they are comparing against
Switch to listing features
items.explanation: The method stays the same; the comparison point changes.

items.prompt: Using the generic figure on a light buyer
choices: Understates their value
Matches their value exactly
Overstates their value
Has no effect on trust
items.explanation: A lighter bottle habit gives a smaller true number.

items.prompt: Hiding a real downside behind value language
choices: Builds a stronger long-term deal
Makes the pitch more honest
Sets up disappointment and lost trust
Is required in every pitch
items.explanation: Honest framing includes real trade-offs.

items.prompt: Who is a good example of a different top rung?
choices: A buyer of two bottles a day who wants savings
A buyer who simply wants a larger kind of bottle
A home-coffee drinker who wants cleaner taste
A buyer who only ever reads the spec sheets
items.explanation: Their goal is taste in coffee, not savings on bottles.

items.prompt: The worked example in L3 is
choices: The only valid way to pitch
A rule that applies to every pitch
A case, not the whole territory
A pitch with no assumptions
items.explanation: The same method applies to many products and listeners.

items.prompt: A listener already owns a different filter and never buys bottles. Which line is the best opening?
choices: 'You will save $1,028.50 compared with buying bottles'
'It holds ten cups and the plastic is BPA-free, too'
'It uses activated carbon to remove chlorine taste'
'Your filters last longer, so you replace them less'
items.explanation: The best opening is in the listener's terms and compares to what they own. The bottle saving cannot apply to them.
items.reference:
Same pitcher, different listeners
🥤 Buys two bottles a day: $1,028.50 saved
☕ Drinks only home coffee: cleaner taste
🚰 Owns another filter: cheaper per gallon
Why: value is set by what this listener compares the product against.
items.learnMore:
Find what this listener is comparing against

A generic figure overstates value for light buyers and cites a saving that cannot be realised by people who never buy bottles. The method is constant; the top rung changes.

Common mistake

Reusing the headline figure on every listener, or hiding a real downside behind value language.
items.reflection: Think of a product pitched to you with someone else's use case. What would have been the right top rung for you?

items.prompt: A listener buys one bottle a day at $1.50. What is a correct year-one saving for them?
choices: $1,028.50, since the pitcher is the same
$547.50, since filters cost them nothing
$514.00, since half the cost is saved
items.explanation: One bottle a day costs 1.50 x 365 = 547.50, and 547.50 - 66.50 = 481.00. Halving the bottle habit roughly halves the saving.
